This vignette is the reference for **Figure 1** of the paper. It sets out the
simulation in enough detail to be reproduced, defines the three
PIT-Wasserstein metrics briefly, and reads the four panels. The paper states
the same material compactly in its methods section and refers back here for
the full specification.

If you are new to calibration or to the probability integral transform, read
`vignette("introduction-to-pit")` first. For the null distributions and
$p$-values, see `vignette("significance-testing")`.

# 1. The simulation

The difficulty in evaluating a calibration metric is that real forecasters do
not come with their miscalibration written on the label. So we simulate
estimators whose failure mode we fix by construction, and ask what each metric
reports.

## 1.1 The error-function model

Each simulated **estimator** is defined by two distributions, following the
structure introduced in `vignette("introduction-to-pit")`:

| Component | Symbol | Role |
|---|---|---|
| error distribution | $\mathcal{E} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_\mathcal{E}, \sigma_\mathcal{E})$ | how far the estimator's central estimate lands from the truth |
| spread distribution | $\mathcal{S} \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(\sigma_\mathcal{S}, \kappa_\mathcal{S})$ | what uncertainty the estimator *claims* |

For each of the estimator's predictions $i$ we draw a true value $x_i$, an
error $e_i \sim \mathcal{E}$ and a claimed uncertainty $s_i \sim \mathcal{S}$,
and emit the probabilistic prediction

$$
\hat{X}_i \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_i + e_i,\; s_i\right)
$$

Three parameters therefore control everything, and they are independent:

- $\mu_\mathcal{E}$ — **bias**. The systematic displacement of the central
  estimate. Zero means unbiased.
- $\sigma_\mathcal{S}/\sigma_\mathcal{E}$ — **dispersion calibration**, written
  `calibration` in the code and plotted on every x-axis below. This is the
  ratio of the uncertainty the estimator *claims* to the uncertainty it
  actually *has*. One is perfect; below one is over-confident; above one is
  conservative.
- $\kappa_\mathcal{S}$ — **spread–error decoupling**, labelled "CI variation"
  in the figures. The coefficient of variation of the claimed uncertainty.
  Zero means every prediction claims the same width. Larger values mean the
  stated uncertainty varies from prediction to prediction *without tracking
  the realised error*, which is miscalibration even when the average width is
  right.

The spread distribution is lognormal (`lnorm4`, parametrised by median and
coefficient of variation) because a claimed uncertainty must be positive and
because it makes $\kappa_\mathcal{S}$ scale-free.

## 1.2 The parameter sweep

We simulate **1000 estimators**, each making **1000 predictions**, with the
three parameters drawn independently so that the whole space is covered rather
than a grid of special cases:

| Parameter | Drawn as | Range |
|---|---|---|
| true values $x_i$ | $\mathrm{Uniform}(-1, 1)$ | per prediction |
| bias $\mu_\mathcal{E}$ | $\mathrm{Uniform}(-1, 1)$ | per estimator |
| error scale $\sigma_\mathcal{E}$ | $\log$-uniform | $[\tfrac12, 2]$ |
| claimed scale $\sigma_\mathcal{S}$ | $\log$-uniform | $[\tfrac12, 2]$ |
| decoupling $\kappa_\mathcal{S}$ | $\mathrm{Uniform}(0, 2)$ | per estimator |

Drawing $\sigma_\mathcal{S}$ and $\sigma_\mathcal{E}$ independently and
log-uniformly gives a dispersion calibration ratio spanning $[\tfrac14, 4]$,
symmetric on the log scale — which matters, because an estimator twice too
wide and one twice too narrow are equally wrong and the metric should say so.

Crucially, **bias is drawn independently of dispersion calibration**. Each
point in the figures is an estimator with its own arbitrary combination of the
three, so if a metric conflates bias with dispersion error it will show up as
vertical scatter coloured by bias.

```{r}
bias_limit = 1
conf_range = 2

config = tibble(
  sd_sd_mean = c(conf_range),
  sd_label = forcats::as_factor(c("heterogenous CIs"))
) %>%
  group_by(sd_label, sd_sd_mean) %>%
  reframe(
    samples = 1000,
    bias_dist = "norm",
    bias_location = runif(1000, -bias_limit, bias_limit),
    bias_scale = exp(runif(1000, -log(conf_range), log(conf_range))),
    sharpness_dist = "lnorm4",
    sharpness_location = exp(runif(1000, -log(conf_range), log(conf_range))),
    sharpness_scale = runif(1000, 0, sd_sd_mean)
  )
```


`generate_simulation()` expands that configuration into 1000 × 1000 individual
predictions, and `prediction_scores()` collapses each estimator's 1000
predictions back to one row of scores.

```{r}
sim = config %>% generate_simulation(true_value_fn = function(n) runif(n, -1, 1))
scores = sim %>% prediction_scores()
```

# 2. The metrics

Full definitions and derivations are in the paper; this is the working
summary. For each estimator, the PIT values $u_i = F_i(x_i)$ are sorted and
compared against the uniform plotting positions $r_i = (i - \tfrac12)/n$:

$$
B_{pit} = \frac1n\sum_i \left| r_i - u_{(i)} \right|
$$

which is the 1-Wasserstein distance between the empirical PIT distribution and
$\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$ — the area between the PIT histogram's cumulative
curve and the diagonal. It is zero for a calibrated estimator and grows with
*any* departure, including a pure bias.

The **bias adjustment** estimates one location shift,
$\hat\delta = \mathrm{median}_i(g(m_i) - g(x_i))$ on the link scale, applies
it to the observations, and recomputes the PIT values as $u^{adj}$. Applying
the same two summaries to the adjusted values gives

$$
U_{pit} = \frac1n\sum_i \left| r_i - u^{adj}_{(i)} \right|,
\qquad
D_{pit} = \frac1n\sum_i \left( r_i - u^{adj}_{(i)} \right)\mathrm{sgn}\!\left(\tfrac12 - r_i\right)
$$

$U_{pit}$ is the same undirected distance with the location error removed.
$D_{pit}$ replaces the absolute value with a weight that is $+1$ below the
median and $-1$ above it, so that departures at the two ends **cancel instead
of accumulating** — which is what makes it signed, and positive for an
over-confident estimator.

| Metric | Range | Reads |
|---|---|---|
| $B_{pit}$ | $[0, \tfrac12]$ | total miscalibration, bias included |
| $U_{pit}$ | $[0, \tfrac12]$ | miscalibration with bias removed |
| $D_{pit}$ | $[-\tfrac14, \tfrac14]$ | signed dispersion error: $+$ over-confident, $-$ conservative |

All three are returned by `prediction_scores()` alongside the mean CRPS and
coverage probabilities.

# 3. Figure 1

The four panels plot each of the 1000 estimators against its true dispersion
calibration $\sigma_\mathcal{S}/\sigma_\mathcal{E}$ on a log x-axis, with the
vertical line at 1 marking perfect calibration. A metric that measures
dispersion calibration should form a tight, monotone curve about that line;
scatter is the metric responding to something else.

```{r}
# estimator SD/error SD:
# ratio between the SD of an estimate and the SD of the error function
# a low value means that the estimate is more confident than it should be
# a high value says it is too conservative

# Panel A: mean CRPS

p2a = ggplot(
  scores,
  aes(x = calibration, y = mean_crps, colour = abs(bias))
) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Absolute bias",option = "magma") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "conservative >",
    x = 1,
    y = Inf,
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 1.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< overconfident",
    x = 1,
    y = Inf,
    hjust = 1.5,
    vjust = 1.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  ylab("Mean CRPS") +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  xlab("estimator SD/error SD")

# Panel B: baseline PIT-Wasserstein

p2b = ggplot(
  scores,
  aes(x = calibration, y = B_pit, colour=abs(bias))
) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Absolute bias", option = "magma") +
  xlab("estimator SD/error SD") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< better",
    x = 1,
    y = 0,
    hjust = -1.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    angle = 90,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "conservative >",
    x = 1,
    y = 0,
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< overconfident",
    x = 1,
    y = 0,
    hjust = 1.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  ylab("baseline\nPIT wasserstein")

# Panel C: undirected PIT-Wasserstein

p3a = ggplot(
  scores,
  aes(x = calibration, y = U_pit, colour=sharpness_scale)
) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "CI variation") +
  xlab("estimator SD/error SD") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< better",
    x = 1,
    y = 0,
    hjust = -1.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    angle = 90,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "conservative >",
    x = 1,
    y = 0,
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< overconfident",
    x = 1,
    y = 0,
    hjust = 1.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  ylab("undirected\nPIT wasserstein")

# Panel D: directed PIT-Wasserstein

p3b = ggplot(
  scores,
  aes(x = calibration, y = D_pit, colour=sharpness_scale)
) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  # facet_wrap(~sd_label)+
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "CI variation") +
  xlab("estimator SD/error SD") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "overconfident >",
    x = 1,
    y = 0,
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    angle = 90,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< conservative",
    x = 1,
    y = 0,
    hjust = 1.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    angle = 90,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "conservative >",
    x = 1,
    y = 0,
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< overconfident",
    x = 1,
    y = 0,
    hjust = 1.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  ylab("directed\nPIT wasserstein")

## Combined 4 panel plot

plot_metrics = patchwork::wrap_plots(
  p2a,
  p2b,
  p3a,
  p3b,
  ncol = 2,
  guides = "collect",
  axes = "collect"
) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

.gg_save_as(
  plot_metrics,
  file.path(fig_dir, "fig1-metric-compare"),
  size = std_size$two_third,
  formats = c("pdf", "eps")
)
```

**Panel B, Mean CRPS** The CRPS is a *proper score* and the standard summary of 
probabilistic forecast quality. Points are coloured by absolute bias.

It does respond to dispersion calibration — the lower envelope of the cloud
has a minimum near 1 — but the response is swamped. For any given value on
the x-axis the CRPS varies by a factor of several, ordered almost entirely by
**colour**: the dark points (unbiased) sit low and the light points (badly
biased) sit high. CRPS is dominated by accuracy, which is what a proper score
is for. Two estimators with identical dispersion calibration score very
differently if one is biased, and an unbiased over-confident estimator can
outscore a well-dispersed biased one.

This is the gap the rest of the figure addresses. CRPS answers "which
forecaster is better?"; none of these panels is trying to answer that. They
ask "*how* is this forecaster wrong?", which a single proper score cannot be
expected to decompose.

Reading the three PIT-Wasserstein panels together:

**Panel B, $B_{pit}$** (coloured by absolute bias) has the same V shape
but, like CRPS, is stratified by colour: bias inflates it. $B_{pit}$ is the
honest omnibus statistic — it answers "is anything wrong?" and a location
error genuinely is something wrong — but it cannot tell you *what*.

**Panel C, $U_{pit}$** (coloured by CI variation aka skill-spread decoupling) is 
the same statistic after the bias adjustment. The colour stratification is gone:
the points collapse onto a tight V with its minimum at 1. **This is the central
claim of the paper made as a picture** — the same estimators, the same arbitrary
biases, and the metric now responds to dispersion calibration alone. What
vertical spread remains is ordered by the colour scale, i.e. by
$\kappa_\mathcal{S}$: spread–error decoupling lifts the floor of the V above
zero, correctly, because an estimator whose stated uncertainty varies without
tracking its error is not calibrated however good its average width.

**Panel D, $D_{pit}$** (coloured by CI variation)  is the signed version, and it crosses zero —
monotonically — at exactly the point of perfect calibration. Negative is
conservative, positive is over-confident, so the sign names the failure rather
than merely detecting it. Two further properties are visible: the root does
not move with $\kappa_\mathcal{S}$ (the colours are mixed where the curve
crosses zero, unlike in panel C), and the curve is close to symmetric about
the crossing on the log scale.

Together C and D are complementary rather than redundant: $D_{pit}$ locates
and signs a width error, $U_{pit}$ picks up shape departures that $D_{pit}$
cancels away. `vignette("significance-testing")` turns that pairing into a
formal procedure.

The one-line summary: **colour stratification in panels A and B reflects bias
, and in C and D reflects spread-skill decoupling.** That is the bias invariance 
the adjustment buys, and it is what makes the adjusted metrics diagnostic 
rather than merely descriptive.

## 3.5 An aside: coverage probability

The obvious alternative diagnostic is to ask how often the truth falls inside
a stated interval. For comparison:

```{r}

ggplot(
  scores,
  aes(x = calibration, y = mean_coverage.0.5, colour=sharpness_scale)
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "conservative >",
    x = 1,
    y = 0.5,
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    angle = 90,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< overconfident",
    x = 1,
    y = 0.5,
    hjust = 1.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    angle = 90,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "conservative >",
    x = 1,
    y = 0.5,
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "label",
    label = "< overconfident",
    x = 1,
    y = 0.5,
    hjust = 1.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  ylab("50% coverage probability") +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "CI variation") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  xlab("estimator SD/error SD")
```

Coverage is monotone in dispersion calibration and has the right sign, so it
is a usable diagnostic. Two things limit it. It saturates — the curve flattens
at both ends, so it discriminates poorly among badly miscalibrated or biased
estimators — and it is a single binary summary at one nominal level, throwing
away everything the rest of the predictive distribution says. The
PIT-Wasserstein metrics use the whole distribution and do not saturate.
